source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Solution rates and times follow the predicted difficulty order in matchstick arithmetic: loose-chunk value change (A) easiest, tight-chunk (C) harder, operator change (B) hardest. Eye tracking did not disturb this pattern.
numbers: N=24 students, one trial per problem, 5 min limit. Solved: A 23/24, C 18/24, B 9/24. A vs B chi2(1)=18.38 p<.001; A vs C chi2=4.18 p<.05; C vs B chi2=4.78 p<.05. Median solve time A 22 s, C 136 s, B 300 s (cap). C faster than B T=36 p<.05. Authors say results match Knoblich et al. 1999 run without eye tracking.
limits: Three items, one per type, so problem type and item are confounded. Difficulty tracks how much of the usual arithmetic frame must be dropped.
agent_relevance: Rank the constraints a task imposes by how deeply they are baked into the default frame. Expect the deepest constraint to cost the most; budget for it.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Mean fixation duration is longer on the hard problems and grows over time, as a stuck state (impasse) predicts. But it does not separate eventual solvers from non-solvers.
numbers: Problem main effect F(2,44)=3.49 p<.05 (B and C longer than A, both p<.05). Interval main effect F(2,44)=8.58 p<.001. No interaction F(4,88)=1.54 p=.20. No difference in fixation duration between successful and unsuccessful solvers.
limits: Fixation length marks being stuck on any account (functional fixedness, mental set, progress monitoring). It cannot tell the theories apart. Authors concede this.
agent_relevance: A pure 'I am stuck' signal (longer, slower steps) is weak evidence of anything specific. Use it only to trigger a reframe attempt, never to choose which reframe.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: At the start, attention goes to the numbers (values) and away from the plus and equals signs. This holds on all three problems. It is the signature of the wrong initial frame.
numbers: Long fixations only (above median). Element main effect F(3,63)=24.02 p<.001; no problem effect p=.42; interaction F(6,126)=2.06 p=.06. Result > operands > plus and equals signs; plus and equals below the 20% chance share. Short fixations showed no such bias.
limits: Effect appears in the long (deep processing) fixations, not short re-encoding glances. A median split on fixation length is a post hoc choice.
agent_relevance: The first representation spends effort on the elements that look like data. The elements that look like syntax or glue get ignored. A reframe step should list the glue elements explicitly.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Solvers shift attention to the critical element late, just before solving. Non-solvers never do. This fits a late re-representation.
numbers: Problem B (operator is key), long fixations: success x interval interaction F(1,22)=7.91 p<.01; interval F(2,44)=12.35 p<.001; share on operators rose above chance in interval 3 for solvers only. Short fixations: solvers higher on operators in intervals 1-2, contrast F(1,22)=7.09 p<.05. Problem C (X symbol is key): long fixations interaction F(2,42)=5.08 p<.05, interval F(2,42)=5.31 p<.01; shift to the result appeared only in interval 3. Short fixations on C: success effect only marginal, F(1,21)=3.09 p=.09.
limits: Only 3 intervals per solver. Graf et al. 2023 later argued ANOVA on bins blurs the timing. Short-fixation effects were weak.
agent_relevance: Success is marked by a move of focus onto the element that breaks the frame, not by more effort in general. A checkable trace: does the attempt now touch the element that earlier attempts ignored?

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Authors argue only representational change explains the whole pattern: longer stuck state, initial bias to values, then a late shift to the critical element. Rival principles each explain one piece.
numbers: Rivals named: functional fixedness, mental set, Einstellung, insufficient progress (MacGregor et al. 2001), Gestalt restructuring, variation-selection, gradual transformation of past experience. All predict longer fixations at impasse; none predicts the specific attention path.
limits: Argument by conjunction on N=24 and one task family. Never tested against a rival model fitted to the same data. Not a decisive test.
agent_relevance: Weak support for specific mechanisms. Treat 're-representation' as a plausible operator, not a proven law.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Original four-experiment test of the theory. Impasses are broken by relaxing constraints on the solution or by decomposing perceptual chunks. The two mechanisms predict problem difficulty and differential transfer.
numbers: Abstract only read (via OpenAlex). Four experiments with matchstick arithmetic. No numbers read this session.
limits: Abstract only. Cited 613 times per OpenAlex.
agent_relevance: Core source for the two mechanisms. Our operators O4/O6 should map to these two: drop a stated constraint, or split a unit into parts.

source: Wu, He, Zhou, Xiao & Luo (2017) Decomposing a chunk into its elements and reorganizing them as a new chunk
finding: Chunk decomposition has two sub-steps. Taking a tight chunk apart is harder (decomposition), but regrouping the pieces into a new chunk is not harder for tight chunks. So tightness explains only the first step.
numbers: N=60 students (two parts). Decomposition task: radical (loose) 98.4% accuracy, 1,797 ms; stroke (tight) 90.0%, 3,070 ms. Reorganization task: radical 49.8%, 4,730 ms; stroke 49.2%, 4,245 ms. RT task main effect F(1,24)=45.77 p<.001 partial eta2=0.66.
limits: Chinese characters, not matchsticks. Authors invoke global-first perception to explain why tight stroke-level regrouping is not harder. Single lab.
agent_relevance: Splitting a unit and rebuilding it are separate steps with separate failure rates. Breaking apart succeeded 90-98% here, regrouping only about 50%. A reframe loop needs a recombination check, not only a break-it-up step.

source: Wu, He, Zhou, Xiao & Luo (2017) Decomposing a chunk into its elements and reorganizing them as a new chunk
finding: A pure organization task (no decomposition needed) was solved about 62-64% of the time with no tightness effect on accuracy, but tight (stroke) items were solved faster.
numbers: Accuracy radical 62.2% vs stroke 64.2%, t(25)=0.79 p=.44 d=0.17; RT radical 6,405 ms vs stroke 5,602 ms, t(25)=3.52 p=.002 d=0.56.
limits: Small, within-subject, Chinese character material. The faster stroke condition is unexplained beyond global-first perception.
agent_relevance: Even when the pieces are handed over, regrouping fails about 4 times in 10. A pieces list is not enough; the new grouping must be searched for.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov & Ardislamov (2025) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra
finding: Failed replication of the claim that hands-on interaction boosts matchstick-algebra insight. In three experiments (real sticks, pencils, VR) participants rarely solved by moving things, and solution rates did not rise.
numbers: Exp1 N=105, Exp2 N=88, Exp3 N=73 (Roman numeral screening). Bayesian logistic regression: nearly all interactivity contrasts had 95% intervals spanning zero (ROPE share 36-71%). Mean movements per problem in Exp1: A 0.56, B 1.70, C 1.91, D 8.26. One exception: interactive sticks helped problem D in Exp2, and VR interactive sticks in Exp3.
limits: Conceptual replication, one lab family, mostly women (about 80%) university students. Positive effect appears only for the problem that needs chunk work on X and V.
agent_relevance: Acting on the object helps only when the action matches the needed change. For code, running something may help chunk problems but can lock in the old frame for constraint problems.
quote: Authors: movements did not contribute to chunk decomposition but significantly interfered with relaxation of higher-level constraints.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov & Ardislamov (2025) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra
finding: The difficulty order from the theory replicated again. Type A is easy. Types B, C, D are much harder, with C the hardest.
numbers: Bayesian logistic regression vs problem A (intercept 1.81 log-odds): B -1.59 [-2.07,-1.17], C -2.95 [-3.40,-2.54], D -1.93 [-2.40,-1.51]; 0% of each posterior in the null zone. Pooled N about 266 across three experiments (my sum).
limits: Pooled over three experiments. Task difficulty is partly confounded with item features.
agent_relevance: Safe to treat 'how many constraints must go' as a difficulty predictor. Count constraints to forecast effort.

source: Macchi, Inglese, Caravona et al. (2026) Does physical interaction with insight problems really affect the solution rate?
finding: Hands-on material gave no gain on a spatial insight problem (pencil version of the match problem). But a picture of real matchsticks, with overlapping sticks forming the plus, raised matchstick arithmetic solution from 47% to 79%.
limits: Authors favour a 'misunderstanding theory' rival: restructuring is fixing the mis-framed goal. The photo shows the plus can be taken apart, so it is also compatible with chunk decomposition. Between-subject; small cells.
agent_relevance: A hint that shows decomposability gave +32 points. Showing the structure beat acting on the material. Strong sign for a 'show the parts' reformulation step.

source: Macchi, Inglese, Caravona et al. (2026) Does physical interaction with insight problems really affect the solution rate?
finding: As reported by this paper, earlier interactivity effects are unstable: control rates for the same problem vary hugely between labs, and larger samples show no gain except for the eight-coin problem.
numbers: Reported second hand: cheap necklace control 3% in one study vs 43% in another; triangle of coins control 22% vs 85% vs 43%; triangle of coins with one-answer rule 70% vs 46%, but with unlimited answers 68% vs 65%; nine insight problems, paper vs interactive, no difference except eight coins.
limits: Second-hand summary of other papers; I did not open those. Treat the numbers as leads.
agent_relevance: Single-paper insight 'interventions' have wide control-rate swings. Our schema tests should compare against a stable plain baseline over many items and seeds.

source: Macchi, Inglese, Caravona et al. (2026) Does physical interaction with insight problems really affect the solution rate?
finding: Reformulating the question to state the real goal can remove the misframing. In a bat-and-ball style item, asking for the cost of both objects raised correct answers from 10% to 90%.
numbers: Reported by Macchi et al. (second hand): 90% vs 10% correct. Original study not identified or opened.
limits: Second-hand; source study unchecked. Only one item type.
agent_relevance: Strongest reformulation effect seen so far, but unverified. Goal restatement is cheap to test on our own tasks.

source: Luft, Zioga, Banissy & Bhattacharya (2017) Relaxing learned constraints through cathodal tDCS on the left DLPFC
finding: Cathodal brain stimulation (dampens left prefrontal rule use) raised solving only on the hardest matchstick type (C, two constraints to drop). Other types showed no effect.
numbers: N=60 (20 per anodal, cathodal, sham). Post-test type C solved: cathodal 32% vs anodal 5% vs sham 5%, chi2=7.02 p=.030. Type A at ceiling; B and D no group difference. 12 problems before and 12 after, 2 min each.
limits: Small cells; type C pre-test solvers excluded; 2 min limit gave lower C rates than earlier studies. Brain stimulation is not an agent intervention.
agent_relevance: Suggests learned rule use is what blocks the hardest reframes. Relaxing rule-following matters only when many rules must drop.

source: Luft, Zioga, Banissy & Bhattacharya (2017) Relaxing learned constraints through cathodal tDCS on the left DLPFC
finding: Prior success on related problems can make later hard reframes less likely (mental set). The authors cite work where solving type A and B problems first left under 10% solving type C within 2 minutes.
numbers: Cited second hand from earlier three-experiment work. Not re-measured here.
limits: Second-hand. Direction matches the Oellinger, Jones and Knoblich 2008 mental-set work, which I did not open.
agent_relevance: Order of problems matters. Many easy solved cases in the context may entrench the wrong frame for the next hard one.

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci & Bilalic (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis
finding: Restructuring leaves a sudden trace. Solvers' dwell time on the plus sign jumps late; ANOVA with bins hides this, change-point models find it near the 90% time bin. After a hint, attention to the key operators doubles.
numbers: N=61 (5 male), one matchstick insight problem after a non-insight problem. Only 34% solved in first 5 min; hint added 11 more. Change point near the 90% bin for solvers. After hint, dwell on equals doubled at once, plus sign doubled by about the 20% bin.
limits: Re-analysis of an earlier paper. One problem. Gaze is a proxy for representation. GAM predicts the shift too early; change-point fits better. Hint timing fixed at 5 min.
agent_relevance: The sudden shape is real but only visible with the right method. If we log reframe events, log them as events, not as a smooth score.
quote: Classical statistical procedures such as ANOVA cannot capture sudden representational change processes.

source: Ammalainen & Moroshkina (2022) Where does Eureka come from? Unreportable hints and the phenomenology of insight
finding: Hints the solver cannot report (flashed words) change anagram solving. A misleading hint lowers correct answers. A helpful hint does not raise correct answers but makes the solution feel more sudden and insightful.
numbers: Mixed-effects logit: false hint beta=-0.269 SE=0.129 p<.05 on correct solutions; true hint on insight judgment beta=0.62 OR=1.87 [1.18, 2.95] p<.01; false vs true hint on insight judgment beta=-0.81 OR=0.44.
limits: Anagrams, online, hints flashed twice. Not matchstick arithmetic. The null for true hints on accuracy is a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: Misleading cues hurt more reliably than helpful ones help. A scaffold that restates the problem should avoid leading phrasing; a wrong frame in the prompt costs more than a right one gains.

source: Dygert & Jarosz (2026) Navigating the garden path: evidence for restructuring as a shared process
finding: Skill at fixing a wrong early reading of a sentence predicts creative problem solving (anagrams) even after controlling for working memory and fluid intelligence. It does not predict analytic problem solving.
numbers: Exp1 N=85; Exp2 N=97. Partial r(95)=0.41 p<.001 between anagram accuracy and ambiguous-sentence accuracy controlling modular arithmetic. Unique variance in creative score after WMC and non-ambiguous sentences: delta R2=0.09. Analytic (modular arithmetic) delta R2=0.00 to 0.02, not significant.
limits: Correlational, undergraduates, one lab. Anagrams are one creative task. A shared-process claim, not shown causal.
agent_relevance: Re-reading a mis-parsed input is a trait-like skill separate from raw capacity. Supports a separate recheck-the-parse step for reading tasks.

source: Spiridonov, Loginov, Ivanchei & Kurgansky (2019) The role of motor activity in insight problem solving (nine-dot)
finding: Nine-dot problem: practice that primes the wrong movement pattern lowers solving a lot. Training with turns at the dots cut solving to 37.5% from 78.1%.
numbers: Exp1 N=36 solved 52.8% (19 solvers). Exp2 N=64: overall 57.8%; dot-turn training 37.5% vs non-dot-turn 78.1%, chi2(1)=10.83 p=.001. Correct-angle (45 deg) vs incorrect-angle training 63.6% vs 51.6%, not significant.
limits: I read the results lines, not the whole design; interpret the training labels with care. Motor, not symbolic, training.
agent_relevance: Preparatory practice can entrench the lure pattern (a mental-set effect). Avoid worked examples that rehearse the very move that is the trap.

source: Xing, Lu & Hu (2019) The effect of working memory updating ability on spatial insight problem solving
finding: High working-memory-updating people solved a spatial insight problem faster, but the restructuring itself was sudden for both groups. Updating ability helps the search phase, not the restructuring step.
numbers: Abstract paragraph only. No sample size read.
limits: Abstract only; no numbers. Single problem family.
agent_relevance: Capacity helps the search phase before the jump, not the jump. Extra reasoning budget should go to exploration, not to forcing the reframe.

source: Danek et al. (2016) Solving classical insight problems without Aha! experience: 9 dot, 8 coin, and matchstick arithmetic problems
finding: The more constraints a problem needs relaxed, the less often solvers report an Aha. Many correct solutions to classic insight problems come without Aha, so solving the task is not the same as having had insight.
numbers: Abstract only (via OpenAlex); the PDF was blocked. No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. Self-report of Aha.
agent_relevance: Do not use 'got it suddenly' wording in the agent as a pass signal. Check solutions by test, not by feel.

source: Authors not read (2025) Testing the independence of representational change theory processes, Thinking & Reasoning
finding: Instructions that cue chunk decomposition help only chunk problems, and cues for constraint relaxation help only relaxation problems. Giving both at once did not do better and sometimes did worse. The two mechanisms look independent and even competing.
numbers: Abstract only (via OpenAlex). Study 1: CD instruction improved CD problems only; CR instruction improved CR problems only; combined not better, sometimes lower. Study 2: CD instructions generalised somewhat to non-matching CD solutions; CR instructions did not raise CR solutions; single cues sometimes lowered solutions for the other process. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. The authors say the hints may not have been specific enough. Fits the Oellinger et al. 2008 independence claim.
agent_relevance: A targeted hint beats a generic hint, and stacking both can backfire. The agent should pick one reframe operator per impasse, chosen by a code check, rather than ask for all at once.

source: Oellinger, Szathmary & Fedor (2023) Search and insight processes in card sorting games
finding: A card-sorting game was turned into an insight task. The more a hidden rule differs from standard rules known from prior knowledge, the harder it is to find. Solvers differ in preferred strategy.
numbers: Abstract only. Two online experiments, N=546 total. Hidden rule furthest from prior knowledge was hardest.
limits: Abstract only. Online, new paradigm. Not matchstick.
agent_relevance: Distance from the default frame is a graded difficulty, not on or off. Try reframing operators near the default first.

source: Chao, Hsieh & Wu (2025) Long-distance exploration in insightful problem-solving, Communications Psychology
finding: Using human data (349 usable participants in the first study) and a simulation, problem solving mixes de-fixation and exploration. Broader exploration marks more insightful search.
numbers: Only the summary line and sample size lines read. 372 recruited, 349 kept; 105 on-site participants in a second part.
limits: Word association task (remote-associates style), not a spatial or matchstick task. I did not read the results.
agent_relevance: A search-based rival to sudden restructuring: wide jumps in concept space. Consistent with sampling more distant candidate frames.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight and self-evaluation
finding: On Japanese children's riddles that need re-representation, 38 frontier LLMs scored far below people. Reasoning models did better than non-reasoning ones but still scored about one-third of the human mean.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference on a 120-item subset, n=126, mean 52.9%. Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6% (subset). On the full set the paper's conclusion gives non-reasoning 9.4%, reasoning 19.3%.
limits: Zero-shot, no retrieval. Riddle items are wordplay, not spatial. Human sample is a subset. Abstract and conclusion numbers differ (different item sets).
agent_relevance: Re-representation of language items is a real gap for models even in 2025. Headroom is mostly in picking the right candidate, see next line.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight and self-evaluation
finding: Main failure was verification: the model had the right answer among its candidates and did not endorse it. Model Aha language was common but mostly wrong.
numbers: Verification failures were 5% to 39% of incorrect answers across models with usable thought-logs (abstract). Claude-opus-4 wrote 'Oh! I just...' more than 100 times in logs; Grok-4 also many; cases leading to correct answers were rare; most such ideas were rejected by the model itself. 'I'm stuck' remarks: Gemini-2.5-flash-preview 9, Claude-opus-4 3, Grok-4 2.
limits: Qualitative, informal candidate tracking, small sample of logs. The authors warn logs may not reflect internal computation.
agent_relevance: Supports G5 and G10: a code-side check must pick the final answer, and Aha-style wording must not count as evidence. Candidate generation is not the bottleneck; selection is.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight and self-evaluation
finding: Thinking in the puzzle's own language (Japanese) did not help and sometimes hurt. Longer thought logs did not give better accuracy.
numbers: Grok-4: English-thought 48.8% (40/82) vs Japanese-thought 29.5% (33/112), p=0.0071. Gemini-2.5-flash-preview: about 15 lines per question in English vs about 209 in Japanese; none of 12 Japanese-thought cases correct. Claude-opus-4: no significant difference.
limits: Language of thought was chosen by the model, not randomized, so selection effects are possible.
agent_relevance: A longer or more laborious re-representation attempt is not better. Keep reframe attempts short and test them.

source: Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi & Taati (2023) LLMs are fixated by red herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: Red herrings (plausible wrong groupings) lower LLM performance, the way misleading cues fixate people. Removing them raised GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 scores. More in-context examples did not help.
numbers: 618 connecting walls from 15 seasons. GPT-4 more than 2x the next-best model on solved walls and correct groups but far below human. Connections task: human about 80%. Two ablations (OCW-Randomized, OCW-WordNet) with fewer red herrings: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 performance increased significantly. Few-shot examples ineffective.
limits: The red-herring link is by dataset design, not a direct test of human-like fixation. Per-model table values were partly unreadable from the PDF; not extracted.
agent_relevance: Distractor-heavy inputs reduce accuracy, which fits G11. Restating the task in a cleaner form might strip lures, but there is no direct test here.

source: M-ARC authors (2025) Limitations of LLMs in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning
finding: On 100 clinical puzzles built to break familiar patterns (Einstellung), most LLMs scored below 50% and several near or below chance. Physicians scored 66%.
numbers: M-ARC: 100 questions; human average 66% over five physicians; most LLMs under 50%, several under 20%. o1 and Gemini named as state of the art.
limits: Small set (100) written by the authors; physician pool of five; no re-representation prompt tested. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: Pattern-breaking tasks expose rigid pattern use in models. Use as a test bed for any reframe operator we add.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma & Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: lateral thinking puzzles for large language models
finding: A 1,100-puzzle multiple-choice set built to test lateral thinking against default commonsense. Models lag people, and the gap widens when answers must be consistent across adversarial rewrites of the same puzzle.
numbers: Abstract page only: 1,100 puzzles; human and model accuracy values were not on the page.
limits: Abstract only; exact accuracies not read.
agent_relevance: Consistency across paraphrase is a ready test of whether a reframe is real or a surface effect.
